summary: Defines Augmented BNF, a compact notation many Internet specifications use to describe formal syntax. It covers naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order independence, and value ranges, and adds some core rule definitions. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5234.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for writing things down, like a recipe for how a sentence may be built from words. This notation lets protocol writers describe exactly what a valid message looks like.

questions: how do you write abnf rules
subtitle: A compact notation that Internet specifications use to write down exactly what valid text looks like.

tldr.problem: Internet specifications need a formal way to define syntax, and each used to carry its own copy of the notation.
tldr.mechanism: ABNF modifies Backus-Naur Form with rule naming, repetition, alternatives, order-independence and value ranges, and gives a set of core rules for a 7-bit US-ASCII environment.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4234 was obsoleted by RFC 5234, which now defines ABNF.

today: RFC 4234 has been obsoleted by RFC 5234, which is now the ABNF specification. It had replaced RFC 2234, and its status here is Draft Standard.

sections.title: Why ABNF Exists
sections.content:
Internet specifications often need to define a formal syntax and can use whatever notation their authors like. Over the years, a modified Backus-Naur Form called Augmented BNF (ABNF) became popular. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power.

In the early days of the Arpanet, each specification carried its own definition of ABNF, notably the email specifications RFC 733 and RFC 822. This document pulls that definition into one place that other documents can cite. Compared with the earlier RFC 2234, the changes are small: one corrected phrase in Section 3.7 and some comment continuation lines that now start with a semicolon.
sections.plainLanguage: People used to copy the same rulebook into every document. Now there is one shared rulebook to point at.

sections.title: Rules and Terminal Values
sections.content:
A rule has the form name = elements followed by a line end. A name starts with a letter, followed by letters, digits and hyphens, and names are case-insensitive. Angle brackets are optional. A rule that needs several lines indents the continuation lines.

Rules end in terminal values, which are non-negative integers. They are written with an explicit base: b binary, d decimal or x hexadecimal. So CR = %d13 and CR = %x0D mean the same, and a dot joins values, as in CRLF = %d13.10.

Quoted literal strings are also allowed, but they are case-insensitive and limited to US-ASCII, so "abc" also matches ABC. To get a case-sensitive match, write the characters individually, such as %d97.98.99. How values map to bytes is left to external encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule gives a name to a pattern. Letters can be written as plain numbers, and a word in quotes matches big or small letters alike.

sections.title: The Operators
sections.content:
Listing rules one after another is concatenation. ABNF does not allow white space between elements implicitly, so a grammar that wants it must say so. A slash separates alternatives, and =/ adds alternatives to a rule defined earlier.

A dash gives a value range, as in DIGIT = %x30-39. Parentheses group elements into one strictly ordered element, and the RFC recommends them to avoid misreading mixed alternatives. Square brackets mark an optional element, and a semicolon starts a comment to the end of the line.

Repetition is written <a>*<b>element, meaning at least a and at most b. The defaults are 0 and infinity, so 1*element requires at least one and 3*3element means exactly three. A bare number n before an element means exactly n, so 2DIGIT is a two-digit number.
sections.plainLanguage: A few small symbols let you say this then that, this or that, maybe this, or this many times in a row.

sections.title: ABNF Defined in ABNF and the Core Rules
sections.content:
Section 4 defines ABNF in ABNF itself. A rulelist is made of rules, and each rule is a rulename, a defined-as sign (= or =/), its elements and a line end. An element is a rule name, group, option, quoted string, numeric value or a prose value in angle brackets, which is a last resort.

Appendix B supplies core rules for 7-bit US-ASCII, kept separate from the notation itself. They include ALPHA, BIT, CHAR, CR, CRLF, CTL, DIGIT, DQUOTE, HEXDIG, HTAB, LF, LWSP, OCTET, SP, VCHAR and WSP. Data is represented as network virtual ASCII, in network byte order.

The RFC's Security Considerations section says only that security is truly believed to be irrelevant to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook is written using its own rules, to prove it works. A starter pack covers common pieces like digits, letters and spaces.

data.title: ABNF rule set
data.code:
ruleset     =  alt1 / alt2

ruleset     =/ alt3

ruleset     =/ alt4 / alt5

; same as:
ruleset     =  alt1 / alt2 / alt3 / alt4 / alt5
